# Hierarchical, Graph-Based, and Adaptive Structures

Also called: Adaptive Spatial Partitioning, Elastic Inference, Scale-Adaptive Splatting, Cross-Level Feature Coupling

## Overview
This family encompasses methods that modify the standard flat Gaussian representation to address scalability, memory constraints, and multi-scale rendering artifacts. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), which treats all primitives equally in a single list, these methods introduce structure (graphs, octrees) or dynamics (time-adaptive deformation, elastic selection) to optimize training efficiency, reduce memory footprint, or improve visual fidelity at varying zoom levels.

## Shared principles
The core principle is the deviation from a uniform, static distribution of $N$ Gaussians. Instead, the representation is either:
1.  **Partitioned:** Divided into logical groups (regions, levels) to manage complexity .
2.  **Adaptive:** Parameters are modified at inference or test-time to suit specific constraints (resolution, memory) without retraining the base model .
3.  **Coupled:** Information is shared across structural boundaries (e.g., between octree levels or graph nodes) to maintain consistency .

## Subtopics

### [TraGraph-GS](14454-tragraph-gs.md)
TraGraph-GS addresses memory overflow in large-scale scenes by decoupling training into connected local regions using a camera connectivity graph [14454-tragraph-gs.md]. It constructs a graph $G=(V,E,w)$ where edges represent feature matches, then segments it via BFS into balanced regions [14454-tragraph-gs.md]. Local Gaussians are trained with multi-view and multi-scale constraints, while a coarse global representation avoids densification [14454-tragraph-gs.md]. Novel views are rendered by sorting regions by a matching score and using progressive rendering with an opacity threshold $\beta$ to handle boundary artifacts [14454-tragraph-gs.md].

### FlexGS
FlexGS enables elastic inference, allowing a single model to adapt to varying computational constraints (e.g., VR headsets) by selecting a subset of Gaussians based on a target ratio $e$ [16110-flexgs.md]. Unlike fixed heuristic pruning, it uses a learnable selector and a transformation field trained jointly with the 3DGS model to displace selected Gaussians and compensate for missing details [16110-flexgs.md]. This avoids the need for separate fine-tuning for each compression ratio [16110-flexgs.md].

### [Mipmap-GS](16893-mipmap-gs.md)
Mipmap-GS eliminates aliasing artifacts (spikes at zoom-in, thickness at zoom-out) by deforming pre-trained Gaussians at test time [16893-mipmap-gs.md]. It generates scale-specific pseudo ground-truths by resizing rendered images and optimizes Gaussian parameters (position, scale, color) to match these targets [16893-mipmap-gs.md]. This self-adjusts primitive properties to accommodate arbitrary sampling rates, preserving high-frequency details better than static smoothing filters [16893-mipmap-gs.md].

### [Hierarchical Anchor Coupling](17260-hierarchical-anchor-coupling.md)
Hierarchical Anchor Coupling (HAC) solves feature isolation in anchor-based octree pipelines by establishing cross-level gradient pathways [17260-hierarchical-anchor-coupling.md]. It aggregates context from adjacent octree levels (coarser and finer) using Structure-Aware Containment Aggregation (SACA) and broadcasts a residual adjustment to all visible anchors at a specific level [17260-hierarchical-anchor-coupling.md]. This acts as an implicit regularizer against over-parameterization in dense structures [17260-hierarchical-anchor-coupling.md].

## Background
These methods emerged as 3DGS scaled to larger datasets and diverse hardware constraints. TraGraph-GS targets large-scale urban scenes [14454-tragraph-gs.md]. FlexGS targets mobile/VR deployment [16110-flexgs.md]. Mipmap-GS addresses the fundamental limitation of fixed Gaussian dilation across zoom levels [16893-mipmap-gs.md]. HAC targets structured representations like Octree-GS [17260-hierarchical-anchor-coupling.md].
